doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Growing up in the 1940s-50s on swing and school dances
summary: Born in 1937, with an uncle who sent jazz records, Polcer preferred swing to bebop. He recalls daily noontime dances at high school and Rock Around the Clock.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: You were born in the very hottest part perhaps of the Swing Era —
—when you were born, so I don’t know, maybe that has something to do with it.

Well I don’t know. I was born in 1937 so by the time I began listening to music as a youngster, my father was a trumpet player in a polka band so he had no connection with jazz, but my uncle played with Ben Bernie and traveled to Europe so I had a jazz influence in the family, so I think by the mid-40s I mean I was already listening to records that my uncle would be sending over. And that was a resurgence, well I guess you still had Swing Street going in the 40s. I somehow got interested in the swing rather than the bebop that was coming. So yes I started in the 40s listening.
The bebop at the time was a little more challenging for the listener, it kind of abandoned the dance end of things. Did it have any effect on your listening do you suppose?
Well I don’t know. I guess I didn’t listen too much to it because I really enjoyed this swing and I think even going, when we got into high school we used to have noontime

dances in high school. It was five days a week. The Student Council would charge two cents admission and with that money that they’d collect every day, once a week we’d go out and buy records. And of course at that time there were still Tommy Dorsey’s “Boogie Woogie,” and Benny Goodman and a few others. So in addition to the pop singers in the early 50s, because I was president of the Student Council, I’d go out and buy some jazz records, and kids were dancing every noontime in the gym. It was incredible. It would last a half an hour during noontime. So I enjoyed, I guess what I was saying, I enjoyed the dancing part of it and the swing, and I think I shied away a little bit from the bebop, where the beat got a little bit more intricate and demanded more of the audience. I just got hooked on the interaction of the dancing and the people.
That’s pretty interesting that the high school kids would be doing that much dancing. Nowadays it seems like touching each other —

Well that was the end of that era. It was 1956 when I was in college, when Bill Haley came in with “Rock Around the Clock,” and that was really a jitterbug tune, in fact I think Cliff Lehman, Eddie Condon’s drummer, was the drummer on that album.
Well if you think of it, “Rock Around the Clock,” it was just —
It was just a swinging thing. But from there on, I don’t know what the point was —
We were talking about the kids dancing.

Why they would dance — they did — we did touch dance at that time in the ‘50s. I mean I was in high school from ‘50 through ‘54. And that was wonderful. It was only later on maybe getting into almost the ‘60s where the separate dancing came in.
